title: Designing YouTube at scale
subtitle: From a 4 GB upload to a video that plays on any screen

scenes.narration: People upload more than five hundred hours of video to YouTube every minute.

steps.say: Over a day, that is seven hundred and twenty thousand hours.

scenes.title: Two different problems
scenes.narration: And someone then watches it on a phone in a train, or on a 4K TV at home.

steps.say: Uploads arrive in every format and size you can imagine.
They pile up by the petabyte, every day, and old videos still have to be kept.
And every play has to start fast and never stall, on a weak phone signal or on fast fiber.
So we draw a line down the middle. On one side, the control plane: small web requests, like titles, search and likes.
On the other side, the data plane: moving huge video files. These are two different problems, and they get different machines.

scenes.title: Uploading in pieces
scenes.narration: A creator uploads a four gigabyte file from their laptop. Sending it as one huge request would be fragile.

steps.say: So the app cuts the file into 500 pieces of eight megabytes and sends them one after another, through the gateway.
The ingestion service writes each piece to blob storage as it arrives.
Then the Wi-Fi drops halfway through piece two.
When it comes back, the app asks how much arrived. Sixteen megabytes. It carries on from there, instead of starting the whole file again.
When the last piece lands, the service drops a message on a Kafka queue: a new video is ready. The upload is done, and processing can start whenever there is room.

scenes.title: One file in, many versions out
scenes.narration: A 4K file is far too big for a phone on a weak signal. So workers make several smaller versions of it.

steps.say: A free worker takes the next job off the queue.
It splits the work into branches, one per size: 1080p, 720p, 480p and 360p. Each one is a smaller file.
Every version is then cut into short chunks, four seconds each, so a player can switch between them at any chunk.
Last, it writes a manifest: a small text file that lists every version and where its chunks are.

scenes.title: What the player reads first
scenes.narration: Here is that manifest. It is an HLS playlist, and the player reads it before anything else.

steps.say: Each pair of lines is one version: how many bits a second it needs, its size, and where its own list lives.
The 480p version needs about one point four megabits a second.
And its own list names the chunks, four seconds each, in order.

scenes.title: A phone goes into a tunnel
scenes.narration: Now someone watches on a phone. The player, not the server, picks which version to fetch for every chunk.

steps.say: On good Wi-Fi, the player fetches the first chunk in 1080p.
It times every download. Still fast, so chunk two is 1080p too.
Then the train enters a tunnel, and the next download crawls.
At this speed a 1080p chunk would take 12.5 seconds to load, longer than it plays. So the player looks at the manifest and asks for 480p, which loads in 3.5.
The picture gets softer for a while, but the video never stops to buffer.

scenes.title: Chunks near the viewer
scenes.narration: Chunks are plain files that never change, which makes them perfect for a content delivery network, a CDN.

steps.say: Every video lives at the origin, a big data center, here in the middle of the United States.
Edge servers sit close to viewers, in cities like New York, Frankfurt, Singapore and Tokyo.

steps.callout: popular videos: served from the edge
steps.say: A small slice of videos gets most of the views. Their chunks stay on the edge servers, so a viewer in Tokyo gets them from Tokyo, not across an ocean.

steps.callout: long tail: the edge fetches from the origin once
steps.say: The long tail of rarely watched videos is not kept everywhere. When a viewer in Frankfurt asks for one, the edge fetches it from the origin, and keeps a copy for a while.

scenes.title: A database and a search index
scenes.narration: The control plane has its own stores. The video itself is never in them, only facts about it.

steps.say: Titles, channels and upload times go in a database that spreads across many machines and still keeps them consistent.
Search works the other way round. An index lists, for every word, the videos that contain it, from their titles, descriptions and transcripts.
Search for cat piano, and it looks up both words and keeps the video that is in both lists: number eighty seven.

scenes.title: Counting 100,000 views a second
scenes.narration: Counting views sounds easy. Now imagine a video going viral, with a hundred thousand views every second.

steps.callout: `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1` × 100,000 a second
steps.say: The simple way: every view runs one update that adds one.
But each update locks the row while it writes. A hundred thousand of them a second just queue up behind each other, and the database falls over.
The fix: count in memory first. Each view bumps a counter in Redis, which is very fast.

steps.callout: `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 97850` once a second
steps.say: Once a second, a bot check throws out the fake views, and one single update adds what is left to the row.

steps.say: The creator uploads in pieces through the gateway, into raw storage.
An event on the queue wakes the transcoders, which write chunks and manifests.
The CDN keeps popular chunks near viewers, and each player picks the version its connection can carry.
And beside all that, the small stuff: views counted in memory before they are written, titles in a database, and words in a search index. Two planes, each built for its own job.
